chunks: "CMOS is used so much mainly because of power.
In a CMOS gate the PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down are complementary, so whatever the input is, one of them is off and there's no DC path from V DD to ground.
Static power is basically just leakage. You only pay energy when a node actually switches, about CV squared per charge-discharge cycle.
Older NMOS logic with a resistor or depletion load burned current every time an output was low, which is a non-starter when you have a billion gates.
There are a few other big wins. The outputs swing rail to rail, so you get large noise margins and the logic levels don't depend on transistor sizing.
The inputs are MOSFET gates, so they draw essentially no DC current, which means one output can drive lots of inputs.
And MOSFETs scale beautifully: shrink them and you get lower capacitance, lower voltage and more transistors per mm², and you can put logic, SRAM and analog on the same die.

The trade-offs are that dynamic power grows with frequency and V squared , leakage becomes significant at small nodes, and CMOS inputs are sensitive to ESD and need care with floating pins and latch-up.
But the static-power advantage is the reason it took over."
